newsitem.title: CONGO: Zaire talks bid collapses, Mobutu still in Congo.
newsitem.headline: Zaire talks bid collapses, Mobutu still in Congo.

text.p: Zaire peace talks collapsed on Wednesday but South African President Nelson Mandela and U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun said they would not give up their efforts to prevent a final battle for Kinshasa.

Laurent Kabila's rebel forces said they were continuing their advance on the capital, where a stay-home protest by the opposition to President Mobutu Sese Seko closed shops and markets and all but shut down the usually teeming city of five million people.
Mobutu, weakened by cancer after dominating Zaire for over three decades, had travelled to Pointe Noire in neighbouring Congo expecting to meet Kabila aboard a South African ship moored there.
But rebel leader, waiting in Angola's Cabinda enclave, pulled the plug on the peace talks by saying he would only board the ship if it sailed out into international waters.
It was not clear on Wednesday evening whether Mobutu would return to Kinshasa. A spokesman in Kinshasa said Mobutu's government was still hoping the talks would go ahead.
U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun told reporters on the South African ship where the two men were due to meet that their host, Mandela, had rejected the demand that the ship put to sea.
"President Mandela said the ship will not go to the high sea for the meeting and therefore the meeting will not be held," Sahnoun, who also represents the Organisation of African Unity, said.
Sahnoun said he and Mandela had not totally abandoned hope and pledged further efforts to avert what he called "another humanitarian tragedy".
He said he and Mandela would talk to Mobutu on Wednesday night and would invite rebel leader Kabila to join them for talks in South Africa.
Rebel spokesmen quoted security reasons for Kabila's last-minute demand.

Earlier, rebel Justice "Commissioner-General" Mwenze Kongolo told Reuters by telephone from Cabinda where Kabila was waiting to join the South African ice-breaker SAS Outeniqua that they would attend if the venue was right.

In Kinshasa, Laurent Mbayo, an adviser to Mobutu's veteran political opponent, Etienne Tshisekedi, said the success of the stay at home strike "has clearly shown that the people don't want Mobutu any more, and people know exactly what to do when the rebels come."
Rebel radio suggested that Kabila's forces were nearing the approaches to Kinshasa. The government dismissed such reports.
Just in case, soldiers from five Western armies remained on standby in Congo's capital Brazzaville or at sea off Zaire to evacuate foreign nationals from Kinshasa if need be.
Mobutu, 66, who reputedly amassed a huge personal fortune over the years, seized power in 1965. Western powers supported him as a Cold War bastion against Soviet communism.
The rebels, who took up arms in October demanding Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, now control three-quarters of the impoverished, corruption-plagued nation.
Zairean state television, in its main afternoon bulletin, quoted the government as saying that fighting was going on in and around Kenge, more than 200 km (125 miles) from Kinshasa.

It said the Kwango River Bridge, about 180 km (110 miles) by road from the capital, was still in the hands of Mobutu forces. Rebels and Kinshasa residents in contact with the area said earlier it had been abandoned by the army on Monday.
Switzerland said it was examining a request from the interim public prosecutor in the rebel-controlled Zairean city of Lumumbashi for Mobutu's assets in Swiss banks to be frozen.
